plan.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to take any company's balance sheet, say in plain words what it owns, what it owes and what is left for the owners, check that the two sides match, and spot three warning signs: more short-term debt than cash to cover it, a big pile of unpaid customer bills, and a growing gap between profit and cash.
plan.horizon14: Later, around day 14, you could compare two years of the same company's balance sheet and explain what changed and why.
plan.horizon28: Later, around day 28, you could read a balance sheet alongside the income statement and cash flow statement and tell a short story of the business from all three.

picture.name: A house with a mortgage
picture.line: A balance sheet is a photo of one house on one day: the house and everything in it is what you own, the mortgage and the unpaid bills are what you owe, and whatever is left is yours.

chapters.title: The one equation
chapters.covers: Own minus owe equals yours: assets, liabilities and equity, and why the two sides of the sheet always add up to the same number.
chapters.outcome: You can take any balance sheet, find the three totals, and show that what it owns equals what it owes plus what belongs to the owners.
chapters.hook: Every balance sheet ever written adds up to the same equation. Why can it never be off by a cent?

chapters.title: A photo, not a film
chapters.covers: A balance sheet shows one day, not a year; where the date sits, how it differs from an income statement, and why two dates side by side matter.
chapters.outcome: You can say which day a balance sheet describes and explain why it cannot tell you how much the company earned.
chapters.hook: Assets are listed in a strict order, and the order tells you how fast each one turns into cash.

chapters.title: What it owns: assets, fast and slow
chapters.covers: Current assets that turn to cash within 12 months (cash, stock, bills customers owe) versus long-term ones (buildings, machines, brands bought from others).
chapters.outcome: You can sort every asset line into fast or slow and name the two or three biggest things the company owns.
chapters.hook: A company can owe billions and be perfectly healthy. What matters is when the bills come due.

chapters.title: What it owes: debts, soon and later
chapters.covers: Current liabilities due within 12 months (supplier bills, short-term loans, taxes) versus long-term debt, and reading the amounts and due dates.
chapters.outcome: You can list what the company must pay in the next 12 months and what it can pay later, and name who it owes.
chapters.hook: Some well-known companies have negative equity. Can a business be worth less than nothing and still run?

chapters.title: What is left: the owners' share
chapters.covers: Equity as money the owners put in plus profit kept over the years, why it can shrink or go negative, and why it is not the same as what the company is worth.
chapters.outcome: You can explain where the equity number came from and say whether past profits were kept or paid out.
chapters.hook: Profitable companies go bust every year. The balance sheet shows the reason before it happens.

chapters.title: Three checks in five minutes
chapters.covers: Three quick comparisons: current assets against current liabilities, total debt against equity, and cash against short-term debt; what a healthy and an unhealthy number looks like.
chapters.outcome: You can run the three checks on a real balance sheet and say in one sentence whether the company can pay its bills this year.
chapters.hook: Two companies, same assets, same profits. One is a safe bet and one is a gamble. Which line tells you?

chapters.title: Reading a real one, start to finish
chapters.covers: A full walk through a published balance sheet from a listed company: the order of lines, the footnotes, the odd items, and the three warning signs to look for.
chapters.outcome: You can read a real published balance sheet in 20 minutes and tell someone else what the company owns, owes, and whether anything worries you.
chapters.hook: The last column, last year's numbers, is the most useful one on the page. Here is why.

sources.who: Benjamin Graham and Spencer B. Meredith
sources.why: the plain-words method for reading each line of a balance sheet
the idea that financial statements are a story non-finance people can read

hooksFrom.horizon14: Later, by day 14, you could compare two companies in the same industry and say which one is on firmer ground.
hooksFrom.horizon28: Later, by day 28, you could read a balance sheet alongside the income statement and cash flow statement and tell a joined-up story.

picture.name: A house with a mortgage
picture.line: A balance sheet is a snapshot of a house: what the house and everything in it is worth, how much is still owed to the bank, and how much is truly yours.

chapters.title: The one equation
chapters.covers: Assets = Liabilities + Equity: what you own equals what you owe plus what is yours, and why both sides always match.
chapters.outcome: You can take any balance sheet, find the two totals, and explain in plain words why they are equal.
chapters.hook: Every balance sheet ever written adds up to the same equation. Why can it never be off by a cent?

chapters.title: What the company owns
chapters.covers: The assets side: cash, money customers owe, stock on shelves, buildings and machines, and the order they are listed in.
chapters.outcome: You can read the assets list top to bottom and say which items could turn into cash within a year.
chapters.hook: Assets are listed in a strict order, and the order tells you how fast each one turns into cash.

chapters.title: What the company owes
chapters.covers: The liabilities side: bills due soon, loans due in years, and the difference between the two.
chapters.outcome: You can split a company's debts into due-within-a-year and due-later, and say which pile matters most right now.
chapters.hook: A company can owe billions and be perfectly healthy. What matters is when the bills come due.

chapters.title: What is left for the owners
chapters.covers: Equity: the money owners put in plus profits kept over the years, and what it means when it shrinks or goes negative.
chapters.outcome: You can find equity on a balance sheet and explain where it came from and whether it grew or shrank since last year.
chapters.hook: Some well-known companies have negative equity. Can a business be worth less than nothing and still run?

chapters.title: Can it pay its bills?
chapters.covers: Comparing cash and near-cash to bills due soon, using one ratio: current assets divided by current liabilities.
chapters.outcome: You can calculate the current ratio from any balance sheet and say whether the company could cover the next 12 months of bills.
chapters.hook: Profitable companies go bust every year. The balance sheet shows the reason before it happens.

chapters.title: How much is borrowed?
chapters.covers: Comparing total debt to equity, why some borrowing is normal, and when the mortgage is bigger than the house.
chapters.outcome: You can work out debt-to-equity for a company and say whether it leans on lenders or on its owners.
chapters.hook: Two companies, same assets, same profits. One is a safe bet and one is a gamble. Which line tells you?

chapters.title: Read a real one, start to finish
chapters.covers: A walkthrough of a real published balance sheet, two years side by side, applying everything from chapters 1 to 6 in 10 minutes.
chapters.outcome: You can pick up a real company's balance sheet, read it in 10 minutes, and give a 3-sentence verdict on its financial footing.
chapters.hook: The last column, last year's numbers, is the most useful one on the page. Here is why.

sources.who: Benjamin Graham and Spencer B. Meredith
sources.why: the plain-words method for reading each line of a balance sheet
the idea that financial statements are a story non-finance people can read
